In 2023, [British YouTuber](https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCMb0O2CdPBNi-QqPk5T3gsQ) (and former [World Barista Champion](https://www.jameshoffmann.co.uk/work#/coffee-competitions/)) James Hoffman virtually hosted the [Great American Coffee Taste Test](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1fN_z4-EcOU), during which thousands of people simultaneously blind-tasted the same four coffees. Hoffman has published a [video summarizing the results](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bMOOQfeloH0), as well as [a spreadsheet of anonymized survey responses](https://bit.ly/gacttCSV+)from 4,000+ participants. It includes tasters’ demographics, general coffee drinking habits and preferences, assessments of the four coffees, and more. \[h/t Dan Brady\] (via [data-is-plural](https://www.data-is-plural.com/archive/2023-11-15-edition/))

This assignment explores the five named graphs to explore the relationships between the variables in the coffee tasting data.

Save this document as \`lecture03.qmd\` in a sensible place on your computer.

Let's load the packages we'll need for our coffee tasting analysis. For the setup today, we'll use the packages in the tidyverse. Load them with the following code chunk and install if necessary.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
```

```{r}
 rename(coffeeC_bitter = `Coffee C - Bitterness`) %>%
 rename(coffeeD_acid = `Coffee D - Acidity`) %>%
 rename(coffeeD_bitter = `Coffee D - Bitterness`) -> coffee_clean
```
